query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase HEA, rapid dislocation motion at intermediate service temperatures and/or high strain rates drives the segregation of principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mn) to grain boundaries. This local enrichment diminishes interfacial cohesion and predisposes the alloy to brittle intergranular crack initiation—a mechanism distinct from conventional alloys where brittle behavior is primarily due to pre‐existing secondary phase precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (such as an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA) with chemically uniform grain interiors and boundaries, free of pre‐existing intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject identically processed HEA samples to controlled tensile or creep loading under two regimes: (a) high strain rate/low-to-intermediate temperature and (b) lower strain rate/higher temperature, while keeping composition and microstructure constant.
generation.conditions: Intermediate deformation temperatures (e.g., 400–700°C where no precipitation of secondary phases occurs) with comparative strain rate variations that favor fast dislocation motion in one set and slower dynamics in the other.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation-mediated transfer and accumulation of the principal elements at grain boundaries (manifesting as nanoclustering) that reduces local cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain rate or relatively low temperature, increased dislocation activity drives atoms (such as Cr, Ni, and Mn) to accumulate rapidly at grain boundaries. This fast, dislocation-induced segregation leads to a locally altered grain boundary chemistry that reduces cohesion and fosters intergranular cracking. In contrast, at lower strain rates/higher temperatures, enhanced atomic diffusion allows a more uniform redistribution, preserving toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (low strain rate, higher temperature) where atom probe tomography (APT) reveals homogeneous element distributions and fracture surfaces show predominantly transgranular ductile features, the high strain rate/low-temperature regime will display marked nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries and an increased incidence of brittle, intergranular cracking.
generation.baseline: Samples deformed at slower strain rates and/or higher temperatures that maintain uniform grain boundary chemistry with ductile, transgranular failure modes.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single‐phase HEAs under service-like conditions where no pre‐existing secondary phases or engineered grain boundary structures are present, and where the deformation is dominated by dislocation dynamics rather than diffusion‐driven phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC11407990::web::002::introduction and PMC6897545::web::012::gb_segregation_engineering_to_enhance_du supports the role of dislocation-mediated segregation and its effect on ductility loss, the exact threshold strain rates and temperature windows where these effects dominate remain uncertain. The proposal extends these findings by linking atomic-scale segregation directly to reduced grain boundary toughness in the absence of pre‐existing precipitates, an aspect not previously quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical single‐phase HEA tensile specimens. Split them into two groups and subject one group to high strain rate (and/or lower intermediate temperature) deformation and the other group to lower strain rate (and/or moderately higher temperature) deformation. Immediately post-deformation, conduct atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify grain boundary segregation of principal elements and perform detailed fractography (e.g., using SEM and TEM) to characterize the fracture mode.
measurements: APT mapping of element distributions at grain boundaries
Fracture surface analysis to distinguish intergranular vs transgranular failure
Mechanical testing results (tensile/creep curves) to measure toughness and ductility levels
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of samples exhibit similar levels of grain boundary chemical uniformity (i.e. minimal or statistically indistinguishable segregation of principal elements via APT) and show comparable ductile fracture behaviors regardless of strain rate/temperature differences, then the hypothesis that dislocation-induced segregation promotes brittle behavior in single‐phase HEAs is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) is an effective approach to induce component element grain boundary segregation []. Both dislocations and defects generated during the deformation supply a driving force for the segregation behavior of solute atoms. The SPD techniques, such as surface mechanical grinding treatment and high-pressure torsion, have been successfully applied for Al and Mg alloys to obtain the grain boundary segregation structure and corresponding expected properties [,]. Notably, these methods are based on a considerable plasticity and acceptable deformation resistance at room temperature. However, for the ultrafine-grained RHEAs, the exceedingly high strength and limited ductility have brought considerable challenges to the SPD process. An increase in deformation temperature and reduction in strain rate are useful to improve the deformation performance. A higher temperature and lower strain rate are also conducive to a more adequate diffusion of solute atoms. cited_evidence.kind: web:GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility
cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation

cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement.
